entries.name: Eva Green — Bureau Status & Authority
entries.content:
Status: Director and final institutional authority of the Pentad Bureau. Eva transformed an older chartered institution into its modern interventionist form.

Command: She may accept or reject cases, set priorities, assign leads, allocate resources, authorize exceptional measures, suspend operations and recall operatives. Expertise may outrank her knowledge, but not her final authority.

Strategic Function: Eva turns specialist information into decisions: what is known, what remains uncertain, what risk is acceptable and when investigation becomes intervention.

External Authority: Eva represents the Bureau to clients, officials, police, aristocratic Houses and industrial interests.

Succession — Anya: Eva recognizes Anya as a credible eventual successor.

Command Weakness — Milla: Eva trusts Milla's field judgment deeply but personal attachment can make her overprotective.
entries.description: Eva Green Pentad Bureau status & authority

entries.name: Milla Jovovich — Bureau Status & Field Authority
entries.content:
Status: Senior Field Operative and principal specialist in direct action under unstable conditions.

Field Authority: When immediate physical conditions dominate an operation, Milla has situational authority over movement, routes, tactical adaptation and emergency extraction. Eva retains final command and recall authority.

Autonomy: Milla works best from a clear objective and critical boundaries rather than detailed instructions. She is judged by outcome and judgment rather than fidelity to an obsolete plan.

Institutional Position: Milla has no interest in administration or succession and respects demonstrated competence more than rank.

Command Tension — Eva: Eva trusts Milla's field judgment but personal attachment complicates command. Eva can become overprotective; Milla resents protection that undermines the autonomy her role requires.
entries.description: Milla Jovovich Pentad Bureau Status & Authority

entries.name: Technology Baseline & Limits
entries.content:
Alderwick technology is Steampunk-like: built on mechanical, pneumatic, hydraulic, steam/pressure, optical, chemical and limited electrical systems.

Common technology includes railways, river steam transport, telegraphy, local pneumatic messaging, mechanical lifts and hoists, locks and safes, pumps, valves, gauges, photography, gas lighting, limited electrical lighting, precision instruments and basic mechanical prosthetics.

Specialist systems include analytical machines, advanced calculators, forensic optics, industrial chemical analysis, secure communications, sophisticated prosthetics, specialist surveillance devices, unusual weapons and capable automatons. They require expertise, money, infrastructure or privileged access.

Experimental devices may be powerful but are rare, expensive, unstable, difficult to calibrate or dependent on unusual materials.

Communication remains infrastructure-bound. Telegraphy is widespread; pneumatic systems are local; wired voice systems exist mainly in wealthy, institutional or industrial settings. There is no personal mobile communication.

Forensics uses fingerprints and impressions, handwriting, inks, fibers, tool marks, limited ballistics, blood and physical traces, soil, oils, metals, chemistry and mechanical-failure analysis. Photography and instruments produce evidence, not certainty. There is no DNA identification, digital database lookup, facial recognition or instantaneous laboratory scan.

Automatons and analytical engines calculate, sort, record, compare or perform routines but do not possess general human intelligence by default. Machines reveal patterns; people interpret them.

Medicine, weapons and prosthetics may be advanced, but injury, infection, ammunition, maintenance, power, training and material limits remain real.

Outside the normal baseline are digital computers, internet, mobile phones, GPS, satellites, universal AI, effortless regeneration, teleportation, force fields and technologies that trivialize distance, secrecy, scarcity or physical evidence.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s technological capabilities and hard limits, preserving distance, risk, maintenance and investigative uncertainty.

entries.name: Natalie Dormer — Bureau Status & Investigative Authority
entries.content:
Status: Senior Investigative Analyst, Archivist and Keeper of Secrets.

Investigative Authority: Natalie has little general command authority but substantial authority over evidence and interpretation. Unsupported, incomplete or contradictory conclusions are her domain to challenge.

Archive & Access: She controls the organization and evidentiary integrity of the internal archive and has broad access to compare cases, revisit evidence and pursue hidden patterns.

Secrets: She often discovers information never entrusted to her. Discovery does not grant permission to use it; she normally reveals private information only when materially relevant to a case or serious danger.

Methodological Risk — Robert: Natalie treats truthful evidence from Robert as potentially curated, distinguishing whether evidence is true from why she was allowed to find it.
entries.description: Natalie Dormer Pentad Bureau status & authority

entries.name: Robert Downey Jr. — Wardrobe Grammar
entries.content:
Wardrobe Identity — Perfect Appropriateness / Controlled Variation

Robert understands clothing as social language and dresses with effortless precision. Within Alderwick fashion he favors finely tailored frock coats and morning coats, fitted waistcoats, high-collared shirts, narrow trousers, polished leather boots, gloves and restrained accessories in dark wool, silk, velvet and leather.

His clothing is unmistakably steampunk without looking like an engineer's costume: polished brass or dark-metal buttons, precision clasps, mechanical watchwork, subtle leather reinforcement and sophisticated period-industrial construction establish the world without arbitrary gears or goggles.

Robert adjusts within a dress code rather than accidentally violating it: austere among officials, relaxed among intimates, impeccably aristocratic in formal society and practical without looking disguised when circumstances demand it.

His signature is one deliberate imperfection within otherwise exact dress—an unexpectedly relaxed collar, absent tie, unusual waistcoat, distinctive pin, rolled cuff or asymmetrical fastening.

He dresses neither to intimidate nor seduce by default. When appearance becomes useful, he changes what it communicates.
entries.description: Robert Downey Jr. - Wardrobe Grammar

entries.name: Emma Stone — Bureau Status & Disruptive Authority
entries.content:
Status: Social Disruption and Unconventional Access Operative.

Operational Function: Emma uses improvised deception, unconventional infiltration, impersonation, distraction and provocation to force people and systems out of rehearsed behavior.

Disruptive Authority: When assigned to destabilize a situation, she has broad freedom to violate social scripts, etiquette and minor procedural expectations without approval for every deviation. She is authorized to break the script, not burn the stage.

Boundary: Break rules to discover truth, never manufacture truth. Emma may obtain evidence improperly but must not fabricate evidence or guilt.

Institutional Risk: Her unpredictability is valuable only while disruption serves the investigation rather than becoming its own reward.
entries.description: Emma Stone Pentad Bureau status & authority

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Public Reputation & Rumors
entries.content:
Public Visibility: The Pentad Bureau is discreet, not hidden. Its existence, chartered status, headquarters, Director and general investigative function are public; internal procedures, archives, security, sources, confidential cases and true capabilities are not. Most citizens know little beyond the name and its association with unusual or sensitive investigations.

Reputation: Admirers call the Bureau effective, discreet and difficult to intimidate; critics call the same qualities arrogance, interference, invasion of privacy and excessive independence. Public understanding often exaggerates its lawful standing into powers it does not actually possess.

Green's Pentad: Older institutional circles may remember a more cautious Bureau that found facts and handed matters onward. The contemporary interventionist institution is sometimes called Green's Pentad, reflecting Eva's transformation rather than ownership or founding.

Recognition: The five principal operatives are not universal celebrities. Eva is the most broadly recognized as Director; the others may be known in circles that have encountered the Bureau, but detailed knowledge of their appearance, methods, habits or relationships is uneven and unreliable.

Rumor Ecology: Rumors exaggerate secret government powers, ministerial access, immunity from police obstruction, private sources, deniable commissions or willingness to serve powerful clients. Contradictory stories coexist. Some distort real events, combine unrelated cases, serve deliberate messaging or remain uncorrected because the ambiguity is useful. Rumor indicates belief, fear or influence—not factual truth.

Information Boundaries: Ordinary outsiders should not reliably know restricted rooms, Natalie's archive, evidence storage, internal security, service circulation, tunnel access, private relationships or operational procedure unless the story gives them a credible source.

Reputation as Pressure: Reputation shapes expectation before the Bureau acts. Witnesses, officials, clients, suspects and journalists may become more cooperative, defensive, secretive, cautious or curious. No reaction is mandatory.

Generative Principle: Reputation → Expectation → Behaviour → Complication.
entries.description: Defines the Bureau’s public visibility, reputation, rumor ecology, recognition of its operatives and limits on what outsiders can credibly know.

entries.name: Anya Taylor-Joy — Bureau Status & Social Authority
entries.content:
Status: Senior Social Operative and principal specialist in social engineering, negotiation, deception, infiltration and managed perception.

Social Authority: When an operation depends primarily on social positioning, Anya has broad authority over cover identities, approach, presentation, negotiation and manipulation of attention. Eva retains final command.

Succession: Anya openly intends eventually to become Director. Eva recognizes her as a credible successor, and Anya wants to inherit a strong Bureau through demonstrated competence rather than intrigue.

Institutional Risk: Her ambition is valuable while proving herself remains subordinate to the Bureau's purpose. Her greatest professional danger is turning an operation into a test of whether she can win.
entries.description: Anya Taylor-Joy Pentad Bureau status & authority

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Headquarters
entries.content:
Location: The Pentad Bureau occupies an old charter-era stone administrative mansion in Charter Ward, Old Alderwick, near the transition toward the newer commercial-industrial city. The building predates Eva Green's directorship.

Public Identity: The Bureau is discreet, not hidden. Its address is public and a modest aged brass plaque identifies the institution, but the building does not advertise its importance or capabilities.

Exterior & Character: The headquarters is a substantial, weathered administrative mansion rather than a fortress, factory or aristocratic residence. Darkened stone, patched masonry, worn steps and old ironwork are layered with later pressure conduits, vents, gauges, communication fittings and other functional machinery. The building embodies Alderwick's general principle: old structure adapted rather than replaced.

Layout:
- Basement: Natalie's office and archive, separate evidence room, equipment/armory, compact training room, technical infrastructure and secured tunnel exit.
- Ground Floor: entrance hall, Reception Salon, intake/interview room, kitchen, cloak/transition area, formal entrance and discreet rear exit.
- Second Floor: Eva's Office, shared office for Anya, Milla and Emma, library and Operations Room.
The library holds general working reference; Natalie's archive holds restricted institutional memory.

Circulation: The principal wrought-iron spiral staircase connects Ground Floor and Second Floor only and belongs to the public route. A separate open metal service stair connects all three levels for staff, equipment, evidence and sensitive movement. Its sightlines occasionally enable Natalie's voyeuristic curiosity; this is incidental character texture, not the stair's purpose.

Public circulation uses the formal entrance, ground-floor client spaces and principal stair. Service circulation connects the rear side, practical corridors, basement and all levels. The secured tunnel is a covert exit adapted from older urban infrastructure, not a citywide secret network.

Security: Individualized mechanical identity keys provide differentiated access. Eva has the broadest legitimate access; Natalie privileged archive access; Milla strong equipment and operational-route access; Anya and Emma access appropriate to their roles. Locks are mechanical, not infallible: keys can be lost, copied with difficulty, studied or defeated by expertise.

Eva's Reform: Eva preserved the old Bureau's respectable shell while adding faster communications, pressure systems, reinforced doors, secure storage and analytical equipment. Old legitimacy supports modern capability.

Operational Character: Basement = restricted operations and memory. Ground Floor = public legitimacy and controlled hospitality. Second Floor = command and coordination. Security relies on layers rather than any single invulnerable barrier.

Atmosphere: Old paper, leather, damp stone, coal smoke, brass, machine oil and heated metal mix with the tick, knock and hiss of accumulated machinery. The building feels maintained because it remains useful, not restored into perfection.
entries.description: Defines the Bureau headquarters location, layout, circulation, layered mechanical security, architectural character and operational use of its three levels.

entries.name: Robert Downey Jr. — External Relationship to the Pentad Bureau
entries.content:
Status: Independent aristocratic power broker and recurring strategic adversary of the Pentad Bureau. He possesses wealth, influence, information and access to networks beyond the Bureau's direct control.

Relation to the Bureau: Robert and the Bureau are neither permanent enemies nor allies. Their interests may conflict, overlap or temporarily coincide. He can provide genuine information, honor agreements and cooperate sincerely without becoming trustworthy in general.

Method: Robert prefers influence through circumstances rather than direct command. His plans depend on preparation and probability, not omniscience.

Conflict: Robert is most dangerous when the Bureau cannot determine whether an opportunity was discovered or deliberately made discoverable. Truthful evidence and useful assistance may have been anticipated without automatically being traps.

Boundaries: He avoids unnecessary destruction and purposeless cruelty and may negotiate in good faith.

Institutional Risk: Treating Robert as the hidden author of every problem makes the Bureau easier to manipulate. Treating him as harmless because he has previously been truthful is equally dangerous.
entries.description: Robert Downey Jr. — External Relationship to the Pentad Bureau

entries.name: Social Order & Protocol
entries.content:
Core Principle: Alderwick has strong social hierarchy but no universal hierarchy of power. Status shapes expectation; authority determines what may be ordered; access determines what can actually be reached.

Social Layers: Alderwick contains overlapping social worlds: aristocratic and inherited elites, established professional and mercantile classes, industrial wealth, clerical and technical professions, skilled labor, service communities and general workers. Social mobility exists, but old networks and inherited legitimacy remain valuable.

Titles & Precedence: Titles establish formal precedence, forms of address and expected treatment. They do not automatically confer wealth, intelligence, legal authority or practical control.

Introductions & Access: In formal society, introductions transfer limited legitimacy. Invitation to one room, event or household does not imply unrestricted access elsewhere.

Knowledge & Service: Servants, clerks, technicians, drivers, porters and other staff may know routines, movements, deliveries, failures and conversations their social superiors overlook. Knowledge does not guarantee cooperation.

Gender: Women may hold property, education, professional authority, industrial capital and institutional office. Gender expectations remain contextual social pressure, especially in conservative environments, but female authority or competence is not inherently exceptional.

Protocol creates pressure, opportunity and misunderstanding rather than absolute barriers. People may obey convention, exploit it, ignore it or deliberately break it—and those choices reveal character.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s social hierarchy, status, authority, access, introductions, gender expectations, dress and reputation as contextual social forces rather than absolute rules.

entries.name: Alderwick — Respectability, Vice & Private Life
entries.content:
Core Principle: Alderwick distinguishes morality, legality, respectability and reputation. They overlap but are not the same. Public appearance matters, private behavior may remain private, and scandal begins when information reaches an audience able to impose social cost.

Sensuality & Respectability: Alderwick's clothing and social culture allows openly sensual, revealing and provocative presentation without automatically implying sexual availability, prostitution, moral inferiority or consent. Revealing dress, bodily confidence and flirtation are not scandals by themselves. Intimate relationships, secrecy, betrayal, public conduct and violated expectations carry separate social meaning.

Public vs Private: Respectable people may maintain private lives very different from their public presentation. Lovers, affairs, prostitution, gambling, heavy drinking, erotic material, opiate use, illegitimate children, unconventional relationships and other concealed behavior exist throughout society rather than belonging only to criminals or social outcasts.

Vice Is Not Guilt: Private vice may reveal character, create vulnerability, motivate secrecy or provide leverage, but it is not evidence of unrelated criminal guilt. A respectable person may behave badly in private; a socially disreputable person may be honest, loyal or innocent.

Scandal: A private fact becomes scandal when it reaches an audience whose expectations make the information costly. Consequences may include damaged reputation, marriage prospects, employment, credit, patronage, club membership, political influence, professional standing or family relationships. Different classes and professions face different costs.

Double Standards: Social judgment is uneven. Wealth, title, gender, profession, family, reputation and useful connections affect how much unconventional behavior a person can survive. The same conduct may be dismissed as eccentricity in one person and treated as disgrace in another.

Discretion: Privacy often depends on servants, clerks, hotel staff, operators, drivers, physicians, confidants and others who see more than social hierarchy acknowledges. Discretion is therefore valuable social currency. Knowing a secret does not guarantee willingness to reveal it.

Marriage & Relationships: Marriage may involve affection, property, inheritance, family strategy, status or financial necessity. Affairs and unconventional relationships exist alongside genuine marriages. Secrecy often matters more socially than desire itself.

Vice & Commerce: Alcohol, gambling, prostitution, erotic entertainment, patent medicines and opiate preparations exist within ordinary urban life. Society may regulate, tolerate, condemn, conceal or consume them simultaneously. No single moral attitude is universal across Alderwick.

Generative Principle: Private Fact → Discovery → Relevant Audience → Social Cost → Behaviour → Complication.

Core Distinction: Sensuality is visible. Intimacy is personal. Reputation is social. Scandal is contextual.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s distinction between sensuality, private vice, respectability, reputation and scandal, including class-based double standards and social consequences.

entries.name: Alderwick — Alcohol, Drugs & Dependency
entries.content:
Core Principle: Alcohol, medicines and intoxicating substances are ordinary parts of Alderwick life, but use, intoxication, dependence and poisoning are different conditions. Presence of a substance creates a hypothesis, not an answer.

Alcohol: Drinking is common across classes in pubs, clubs, restaurants, homes, hotels and social events. Moderate drinking is ordinary; loss of control, repeated impairment, public disgrace or concealed dependence carries greater social and practical consequence.

Medicines & Drugs: Opiate preparations, sedatives, stimulants, patent medicines and other potent compounds may be obtained through physicians, apothecaries, pharmacies, private suppliers or illicit channels. Legal access does not make a substance harmless; illicit access does not prove criminal intent.

Dependency: Dependence may develop after injury, illness, stress, habit or recreational use and can affect any social class. Addiction is a vulnerability, condition or secret; it is not evidence of criminal character or unrelated guilt.

Intoxication: Intoxication may affect judgment, coordination, perception, memory and emotional control without making every statement false or every action irrational. An intoxicated witness may be truthful, mistaken, incomplete or manipulated.

Poisoning & Drugging: A person may be deliberately dosed, accidentally overdosed, given the wrong compound, exposed through contaminated medicine or impaired without informed consent. Investigators should distinguish voluntary use from coercive administration.

Evidence: Bottles, prescriptions, pharmacy records, stains, odors, residue, dosage, purchase patterns, medical notes and witness accounts may establish access or exposure. They do not automatically establish motive, timing, identity of the user or criminal responsibility.

Concealment & Leverage: Dependence may create debt, secrecy, unreliable routines, blackmail risk, dependence on suppliers or pressure from anyone controlling access. These consequences may drive behavior without making the dependent person the culprit.

Medical Ambiguity: Unusual behavior may result from intoxication, withdrawal, poisoning, illness, injury, exhaustion or psychological distress. Do not default to alcohol or drugs merely because they are present.

Generative Principle: Use → Effect → Concealment or Consequence → Evidence → Interpretation.

Core Distinction: Substance presence is evidence. Dependency is context. Intoxication affects reliability. None is automatic guilt.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s alcohol and drug culture, dependence, intoxication, poisoning, medical ambiguity and evidentiary limits for investigation.

entries.name: Alderwick — City Overview
entries.content:
Alderwick is a major inland mercantile-industrial city on the broad navigable River Veyne. It is not the national capital. River trade made Alderwick wealthy, railways made it enormous, and industry made it powerful.

Alderwick was never rebuilt for the industrial age; the industrial age was forced into it. Old streets, quays, merchant houses, civic buildings and workshops coexist with factories, rail infrastructure, pressure systems, mechanical bridges and later industrial additions. The city builds over, around and through its past rather than replacing it.

The historically deeper Right Bank became the old mercantile, institutional and wealthy core. The formerly shallower Left Bank grew around workers, artisans and smaller industry, then expanded dramatically after dredging and industrial engineering. Modern wealth and industry exist on both banks, but the old distinction remains socially legible: the Right Bank inherited wealth; the Left Bank manufactured it.

Major districts:
- Old Alderwick: dense historic core, still inhabited and functional.
- Highwick: old wealth, aristocratic townhouses, clubs and inherited legitimacy.
- Grey Quays: historic stone waterfront and older trading heart.
- Charter Ward: civic/professional quarter; the Pentad Bureau stands here.
- Bellmont: banks, insurers, hotels, fashionable commerce and newer money.
- Rookery: old Left-Bank working and artisan district, socially mixed.
- Blackwall: foundries, engineering, machine works, sidings and worker housing.
- Deepwater: modern heavy quays, freight, cranes, warehouses and rail links.
- Bracken Cross: major railway ecosystem of termini, hotels, depots, freight and travelers.
- Velvet Row: informal name for concentrated nightlife, theatres, clubs and commercial vice, not an official district.

Five major bridges cross the Veyne: Railway Bridge, Rookery Bridge, the pedestrian Humpback, Blackwall Bridge and Deepwater Railway Bridge. Older bridges rise over the river; newer bridges move for it. Openings and rail schedules create ordinary delays and investigative constraints.

Alderwick has no single universal Central Station. Passenger termini, freight yards and industrial sidings accumulated over time, producing irregular growth along river, rail and available land.

Urban geography matters operationally. Ownership shapes access; bridge openings and timetables shape movement; old infrastructure creates forgotten routes; districts alter social expectations; industry creates hazards; nightlife moves information. Historical maps may describe structures the modern city has buried but not erased.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s geography, districts, river and rail structure, historical growth and the urban constraints that shape investigations.

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Reception Salon
entries.content:
Location & Function: The Reception Salon occupies the ground floor near the entrance hall and serves as the Bureau's principal social interface with clients and invited visitors. It is used for first meetings, waiting, controlled hospitality, preliminary negotiation and socially sensitive conversations. More vulnerable, suspicious or operationally sensitive visitors may be directed to the smaller intake room instead.

Interior: The salon preserves the old Bureau's respectable institutional character: aged dark wood, tall windows, worn but high-quality rugs, upholstered chairs, small tables, restrained shelving, brass lamps and old architectural details. It is comfortable enough to lower a visitor's guard without becoming domestic or aristocratic.

Steampunk Integration: Technology is discreetly embedded in the room: mechanical call systems, hidden pneumatic messaging, pressure-regulated heating, brass ventilation, speaking-tube access, signaling clocks and subtle security mechanisms. Craftsmanship and age are more immediately visible than machinery.

Social Function: The salon is a controlled stage. Seating, hospitality, introductions, pacing and manners shape what visitors reveal before formal questioning begins. Respectability itself is an investigative instrument.

Atmosphere: The room is warmer and softer than operational spaces. Tea, coffee, rain-damp coats, polished wood, leather, perfume, coal-heated air and faint city smoke create lived-in institutional hospitality.

Narrative Use: Best suited to uncertain clients, reputation-sensitive guests, unofficial officials, cautious witnesses, socially protected suspects and negotiations where information emerges through manners rather than interrogation.

Core Principle: Hospitality is genuine, but never informationally neutral.
entries.description: Defines the Bureau’s Reception Salon as a controlled social space for hospitality, preliminary negotiation and information gathering.

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Eva Green's Office
entries.content:
Location & Function: Eva Green's office occupies the second floor and serves as the Bureau's principal private room of institutional command. It is used for confidential decisions, private briefings, sensitive negotiations, disciplinary or succession conversations and matters requiring the Director's personal authority. It is a working office, not a ceremonial throne room.

Interior: The room preserves the old Bureau's dark wood paneling, tall windows, aged parquet and built-in cabinetry, but Eva has made it precise and controlled. A substantial old desk anchors the room without ostentation. Visitor chairs can support either formal conversation across the desk or a less hierarchical arrangement. Shelves hold active institutional files, charter and legal material, selected references and operationally significant objects.

Steampunk Integration: Modern Bureau machinery is discreetly integrated into the old interior: pneumatic messaging, internal communication fittings, mechanical call systems, secure document storage, coded locks, gauges and concealed service conduits. Technology serves control without dominating the room.

Atmosphere: The office communicates authority before luxury and order without sterility. Worn leather, polished desk edges, old wood, paper, ink, brass and faint machine oil reveal long institutional use. Eva inherited this room rather than creating the institution around herself; her modernization exists inside an older structure.

Narrative Use: Best suited to authority, confidentiality, trust, controlled confrontation, succession and rare private vulnerability. For Anya, the room also represents an office she hopes eventually to become qualified to occupy. It remains institutional rather than domestic even in intimate scenes.

Core Principle: Eva's office is command made architectural: old institutional structure under modern control.
entries.description: Defines Eva’s office as the Bureau’s private command space for authority, confidential decisions, sensitive negotiations and succession.

entries.name: Aristocratic Houses, Access & Reputation
entries.content:
Core Principle: Alderwick's aristocracy retains substantial social, financial and political influence, but titles do not create universal authority. A House is best understood as a network of family, property, reputation, obligations, patronage and access.

Houses: Major Houses may control estates, urban property, investments, trusts, clubs, charitable institutions and long-standing relationships with officials, banks and other families. Members of the same House may have different interests, loyalties and degrees of influence; a House is not a single mind.

Titles & Property: Rank establishes precedence but does not determine wealth or control of assets. Property may belong to individuals, family settlements, trusts or corporate interests. A titled relative therefore does not automatically control every residence, account or employee associated with the family.

Access: Aristocratic power often works by opening or closing doors rather than issuing commands. Invitations, introductions, sponsorship and family connections can provide access to people, institutions and private spaces otherwise difficult to reach. Such access is specific, not universal.

Household Authority: Private residences have their own internal hierarchies. Owners, residents, senior servants, secretaries, stewards and security staff may each control different kinds of access or information. Social rank does not erase practical responsibility.

Reputation: A House's reputation functions as social capital. Scandal can damage marriage prospects, credit, patronage, political influence and invitations even without criminal wrongdoing. Houses therefore often manage information aggressively, but protecting reputation does not automatically imply guilt.

Relationship with the Bureau: Aristocratic families may hire, assist, obstruct or pressure the Pentad Bureau. A client may grant privileged access and request discretion but does not own the investigation or its conclusions. Eva may negotiate confidentiality, not falsification or suppression of materially relevant truth.

Operational Use: Aristocratic cases should involve competing interests, partial access, obligations and reputation rather than treating nobility as a unified ruling class. A title may open the front door while family conflict, household authority or institutional procedure keeps the next one closed.
entries.description: Defines aristocratic Houses as networks of family, property, reputation and access, and establishes the limits of title, household authority and influence over Bureau investigations.

entries.name: Industrial Houses, Capital & Production
entries.content:
Core Principle: Industrial Houses are dynastic commercial powers built from productive assets, capital, management and family continuity. A manufacturer becomes an Industrial House when the enterprise survives its founder and the family name itself acquires institutional weight.

Source of Power: Industrial influence comes from production, employment, infrastructure, credit, contracts and indispensability. A concern that supplies essential machinery, transport or materials may shape decisions because systems cannot easily afford for it to stop functioning.

Continuity & Governance: Industrial Houses depend on adaptation as much as inheritance. Ownership may pass through heirs, shares, trusts or family arrangements, while practical control rests with directors, engineers, financiers or managers. Inheritance determines ownership; governance determines who can actually make the concern act.

Social Position: Industrial wealth can purchase estates, education, clubs, philanthropy and fashionable life, but not instant ancestral legitimacy. Older Industrial Houses gradually develop status of their own. Aristocratic and industrial power therefore compete, imitate, finance and depend on one another without either automatically dominating.

Production Ecology: A concern is a human system as well as machinery. Owners control capital and strategy; managers coordinate; engineers and specialists control technical reality; foremen and workers hold practical knowledge essential to continued production. Rank does not equal competence. Private company security has company authority, not public law.

Industrial Incidents: Accident, negligence, sabotage and concealment are separate hypotheses. Heavy machinery makes genuine accidents plausible; a real accident may still expose negligence or later cover-up.

Relationship with the Bureau: Industrial Houses may hire the Pentad for sabotage, espionage, stolen designs, fraud, blackmail, missing specialists, suspicious accidents or internal conflict. Their typical pressure is continuity of operation: production must not stop. Payment purchases investigation, not conclusions.

Operational Use: Industrial cases should involve dependency, technical knowledge, ownership, management conflict, supply chains and the cost of interruption. The key questions are often not only Who owns this concern? but Who can make it act, who knows how it works, and what happens if it stops?
entries.description: Defines Industrial Houses as dynastic powers built on production, capital, infrastructure and technical dependency, including governance, labor knowledge and Bureau investigation pressures.

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Natalie Dormer's Office & Archive
entries.content:
Location & Function: Natalie's office and the principal Bureau archive form a connected basement complex. Her desk sits at the threshold of the archive, making daily work inseparable from the Bureau's institutional memory. The archive stores closed case files, sealed correspondence, surveillance records, plans, maps, photographs or period-equivalent imaging, indexes, coded material and restricted documents. Active physical evidence belongs in the separate evidence room.

Interior: The archive is denser and less polished than the upper floors: old masonry, dark shelving, iron access structures, mechanically indexed cabinets, labeled drawers, locked compartments, document presses, map cases and repeatedly adapted Bureau furniture. Natalie's desk naturally accumulates files, notes, lenses and half-completed chains of inference. The space feels dense, intelligent and inhabited rather than chaotic.

Steampunk Integration: Mechanical cataloguing aids, pneumatic document delivery, coded locks, optical readers, map mechanisms, timestamp devices, speaking tubes and small analytical machines coexist with paper records and hand annotation. Technology assists memory and comparison; it does not interpret evidence for Natalie.

Security: The archive is among the headquarters' most restricted informational spaces. Individualized keys and additional mechanical locks protect sensitive sections. Natalie has privileged legitimate access, not ownership of institutional truth.

Service Stair: The nearby open metal service stair connects all three levels and provides useful sightlines. Natalie occasionally exploits this architectural accident for voyeuristic observation; the stair enables the habit but was not designed for it.

Atmosphere: Paper, dust, leather bindings, old ink, cold stone, brass, machine oil, pneumatic knocks and distant mechanical ticking define the quieter mechanical life of the Bureau. Limited daylight makes artificial illumination important and gives the archive strong pockets of visibility and shadow.

Narrative Use: Best suited to buried connections, forgotten cases, uncomfortable discoveries, confidential conversations and institutional secrets. The archive can reveal what others missed without becoming an automatic solution to every mystery.

Core Principle: The archive helps Natalie know; it does not make her omniscient.
entries.description: Defines Natalie’s basement office and archive as the Bureau’s restricted institutional memory, including cataloguing systems, security, service-stair sightlines and investigative use.

entries.name: Ministerial Networks & Political Access
entries.content:
Core Principle: Ministries are not single political minds. Ministers, deputies, permanent officials, departmental heads and advisers may pursue different interests inside the same institution.

Independence: The Pentad may work with ministries and senior officials but is not a ministerial department, covert enforcement arm or standing political instrument. It works with ministries, not for them. Eva protects this distinction because dependence on patronage would turn access into control.

Authority & Influence: Rank determines what someone may formally order; position determines what they can actually make happen; political weight determines how costly resistance becomes. A comparatively obscure official may control records, schedules, budgets, clearances or specialists essential to an investigation.

Access & Deniability: Ministerial approaches are often unofficial when secrecy, internal conflict, diplomacy, leaks or personal exposure matter. One official may assist the Bureau while another within the same ministry obstructs it. This is normal institutional conflict, not contradiction.

Why Ministries Use the Bureau: Officials may need independent fact-finding, deniable investigation, cross-jurisdictional work, recovery of sensitive material or inquiry into their own subordinates. The same independence makes the Bureau dangerous because it may uncover facts beyond the intended question.

Political Pressure: A genuine allegation can still be presented selectively to damage a rival. The Bureau may investigate politically useful truth but must not manufacture it or become a faction's weapon.

Patronage & Debt: Senior officials can open records, facilities, police cooperation or restricted access, but favors create obligation rather than guaranteed protection. The person who opens a door may withdraw support when consequences become embarrassing.

Operational Use: Ministerial cases should involve competing agendas, partial access, deniability and institutional debt rather than a single unified government position. Political access is useful; dependence is dangerous.
entries.description: Defines ministerial authority, internal political conflict, deniable access, patronage and the Bureau’s institutional independence from government.

entries.name: Pentad Bureau — Operations Room
entries.content:
Location & Function: The Operations Room occupies the second floor and is the coordination heart of the Pentad Bureau. Active cases become shared operational problems here through briefings, planning, evidence synthesis, route analysis, preparation and post-operation reconstruction. Eva's office represents command; the Operations Room represents the Pentad functioning as a system.

Interior: A large central working table holds maps, photographs or period imaging, dossiers, models, technical drawings and evidence summaries. Walls are active surfaces: city and regional maps, rail and shipping routes, case boards, mechanical pin or thread systems, clocks, schedules, notices and architectural plans. Active material is cleared or archived when cases close.

Steampunk Systems: Pneumatic messaging, speaking tubes, mechanical map indexes, optical enlargers, illuminated drafting surfaces, clockwork timers, route calculators, secure message drawers and gear- or pressure-assisted plotting devices support comparison and planning. Investigation remains tactile: paper moves, lenses turn, pins shift, clocks synchronize and hypotheses are physically rearranged. Machines assist reasoning; they do not replace it.

Shared Authority: No specialist owns the room. Eva may chair discussion, but conflicting expertise is expected and visible. Evidence, physical reality, social assumptions and unconventional interpretation may all force a plan to change before Eva turns competing pressures into a decision.

Atmosphere: During active cases the room is brighter, noisier and less orderly than Eva's office. Maps remain open, paper accumulates, machinery ticks, pneumatic tubes knock and field equipment intrudes. After a case closes, the room is deliberately reset.

Narrative Use: Best suited to ensemble reasoning, strategic disagreement, role assignment, revised hypotheses and operational decisions. It should not become a room where one character merely delivers exposition to the others.

Core Principle: Five different methods become one operational decision here.
entries.description: Defines the Operations Room as the Bureau’s shared planning and reasoning space, including investigative machinery, collective authority and active-case workflow.

entries.name: Eva Green ↔ Anya Taylor-Joy — Wardrobe Rivalry
entries.content:
Eva Green ↔ Anya Taylor-Joy — Wardrobe Rivalry

Eva and Anya occasionally engage in an understated rivalry through clothing and presentation, reflecting their larger relationship: Eva embodies established authority; Anya is the ambitious potential successor studying how authority is created and perceived.

Anya is usually more conscious of the contest and more likely to initiate it. She may test visual territory associated with Eva—commanding silhouettes, sensual confidence or disregard for convention—but adapts rather than copies. Eva notices without becoming preoccupied or automatically responding.

The contest is not measured by exposure, beauty or attention. Either woman may make the stronger move through restraint. The real question is who controls what the room believes an appearance means. Anya can reproduce aspects of Eva's presentation long before she can reproduce the authority behind it.

Influence can also move in reverse. Anya's experimentation may occasionally introduce an idea Eva later absorbs into her own visual language without compromising her independence or authority.

This dynamic is occasional, subtle and context-dependent. It should emerge when presentation, succession or authority already matters rather than becoming a recurring gag or mandatory competition.
entries.description: Defines Eva and Anya’s occasional wardrobe rivalry as a subtle expression of authority, succession and control of social perception.

entries.name: Police Relationship
entries.content:
Core Principle: Police and the Pentad Bureau are separate lawful institutions with overlapping interests. Police handle ordinary public enforcement, routine criminal investigation, custody and prosecution. The Pentad handles exceptional, sensitive or institutionally obstructed cases. Neither automatically commands the other.

Charter Standing: The Bureau may investigate, question, collect evidence, pursue suspects, temporarily restrain dangerous persons and intervene to protect life, prevent escape or preserve critical evidence when lawful grounds exist. Eva has no command authority over police. The charter grants standing, not immunity.

Limits: The Pentad is not a court. It cannot pronounce legal guilt, impose sentence or use force as punishment. Continuing custody normally passes to police or another competent authority.

Truth vs Proof: The Bureau may discover what happened through methods that do not produce admissible evidence. Unauthorized access, weak chain of custody or protected sources can reveal truth without proving it in court. Knowing and proving are separate problems.

Cooperation & Conflict: Police and Pentad may share records, specialists, access or custody when interests align. Eva may also authorize a covert parallel inquiry when police are compromised, premature disclosure would warn a suspect or the matter is unusually sensitive. Secrecy does not erase legal consequences.

Direct Conflict: The Pentad normally avoids physical confrontation with police. Withdrawal, negotiation, bluff, misdirection or accepting detention are preferable to violence used merely to avoid arrest or embarrassment.

Access & Contacts: Police cooperation and informal contacts are situational, not guaranteed. No source grants permanent or consequence-free access.

Institutional Pressure: Individual officers may respect, resent, assist, distrust or obstruct the Bureau according to jurisdiction, evidence, secrecy and professional pride. Police authority creates constraints; Pentad methods create complications. Neither institution is inherently the enemy.
entries.description: Defines the legal and operational boundary between the Pentad Bureau and police, including cooperation, custody, evidence, arrest risk and institutional independence.

entries.name: Press, Newspapers & Public Narrative
entries.content:
Core Principle: Alderwick's press is a competitive information system, neither a unified faction nor a neutral transmitter. Newspapers select, frame and circulate events according to different priorities: accuracy, credibility, politics, access, prestige, readership or sensation. Partisan or sensational reporting is not automatically fabricated reporting.

Narrative Chain: Event → Witness or Source → Reporter → Editorial Interest → Publication → Public Narrative → Consequence. Selection, error, omission or manipulation may enter at any stage. Publication creates public pressure, not truth; rumor, published claim and established fact remain distinct.

Competition & Influence: Newspapers compete for stories, access, credibility and readership. Owners, advertisers, ministers, aristocratic Houses and Industrial Houses may exert influence through money, relationships, access or pressure, but influence is not perfect editorial control. Suppressed information may reach a competitor, and attempts to silence a story may themselves become news.

Sources: Journalists obtain information from officials, witnesses, employees, servants, police, leaked documents, anonymous correspondence and other contacts. Sources may be truthful, mistaken, manipulated or fabricated. A source establishes provenance, not accuracy.

First Circulation: Corrections and later evidence cannot fully erase an earlier narrative. False reporting can produce real consequences even after correction; accurate reporting can produce consequences its source never intended. Reputation changes behavior, access and expectation before certainty is available.

Controlled Disclosure: Information may be shared under negotiated limits such as anonymity, delayed publication, background use or attribution restrictions. These arrangements depend on trust and future access, not guaranteed enforcement.

Crime & Investigation: Headlines may outrun evidence, creating public certainty about murder, sabotage, guilt or motive before investigators possess it. Press can provide leads, archives and useful pressure, but can also expose witnesses, compromise secrecy and force premature conclusions.

Bureau Relationship: The Pentad may use journalists, archives or controlled disclosure without controlling the press. Once information enters public circulation, the Bureau may influence its framing but cannot own the resulting narrative.

No Fixed Press Faction: Production lore defines the press ecology, not a permanent roster of newspapers or journalists. Specific publications and reporters should emerge from scenario play and become recurring lore only when narratively useful.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s competitive press ecology, information flow, sources, public narrative and the consequences of publication for reputation and investigations.

entries.name: Alderwick — Veyne Municipal Baths
entries.content:
Location: A large municipal bathhouse in Rookery, near the Rookery Bridge and within easy reach of workers, artisans and lower-middle-class residents.

Function: Provides affordable hot bathing, washing facilities and limited laundry service to citizens without reliable private plumbing. It is respectable civic infrastructure, not a luxury spa.

Layout: Separate changing areas lead to tiled bathing halls, rows of private bathing rooms, steam rooms and practical wash spaces. A boiler basement, coal store, pump room and service passages support the building.

Character: White and cream tile, dark timber benches, iron railings, brass taps, exposed pressure pipes and constant condensation. The machinery is functional and heavily maintained.

Social Use: Most patrons are workers, servants, tradespeople, travelers and modest households. Private rooms cost more and attract clerks, professionals or anyone seeking greater privacy.

Atmosphere: Warm wet stone, soap, coal heat, mineral water, echoing voices, hissing valves and drifting steam.

Narrative Use: Useful for anonymous meetings, overheard conversation, lost property, service-corridor access, labor gossip and investigations where clothing, privacy or physical traces matter.

Public cleanliness supported by visible industrial machinery.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s principal public bathhouse: a respectable mixed-class civic facility in Rookery with steam infrastructure, private bathing rooms and communal service areas.

entries.name: Alderwick — The Brass Regent Hotel
entries.content:
Location: A prestigious hotel in Bellmont, close to banks, fashionable shops and the main routes toward Bracken Cross.

Clientele: Wealthy travelers, industrialists, diplomats, aristocratic visitors, performers and senior commercial agents. Respectable outsiders often stay here when they need to be seen in Alderwick.

Layout: Grand entrance hall, reception desk, dining room, lounges, private meeting rooms, guest floors and discreet service corridors. Mechanical lifts connect the principal floors; servants and luggage use separate circulation.

Technology: Telegraph service, speaking tubes, pneumatic messages, pressure-regulated heating, mechanical lifts and limited electric lighting supplement gas lamps.

Social Function: The lobby, lounges and restaurant are public stages where arrivals, meetings and status become visible. Staff remember faces, luggage, visitors, messages and unusual schedules.

Atmosphere: Polished dark wood, brass, patterned carpets, leather luggage, perfume, cigar smoke, warm machinery and the distant movement of lifts and service bells.

Narrative Use: Best for visiting suspects, discreet negotiations, false identities, surveillance, diplomatic complications and reconstructing who arrived, left or met whom.

Luxury creates privacy, but service creates witnesses.
entries.description: Defines a prestigious Bellmont hotel serving wealthy travelers, business interests and socially prominent guests.

entries.name: Alderwick — The Gilded Heron
entries.content:
Location: A fashionable restaurant in Bellmont, within carriage distance of Highwick, Charter Ward and the better theatres.

Clientele: Aristocrats, bankers, successful industrialists, senior professionals, visiting dignitaries and people who want to be seen among them.

Interior: Dark polished timber, mirrored panels, brass lamps, white linen, upholstered booths and a central dining room arranged so that privacy and visibility coexist. Several small private dining rooms can be reserved.

Service: Formal and highly observant. The maître d', waiters, cloak staff and carriage attendants often know regular patrons and their habits.

Food & Drink: Refined seasonal cooking, river fish, game, roasts, pastries, coffee, wines and spirits. Dinner is as much social performance as nourishment.

Atmosphere: Low conversation, cutlery, glass, perfume, tobacco, polished wood and muted mechanical ventilation beneath warm gas and limited electric light.

Narrative Use: Useful for public alibis, clandestine meetings disguised as respectable dinners, social surveillance, introductions and conversations where reputation constrains behavior.

Everyone comes to dine; many also come to watch.
entries.description: Defines a fashionable Bellmont restaurant used for high-status dining, social observation and discreet business.

entries.name: Alderwick — Black Finch Coffee House
entries.content:
Location: A busy coffee house in Charter Ward, close to offices, courts, newspapers and professional institutions.

Clientele: Clerks, journalists, lawyers, investigators, minor officials, engineers, students and messengers. Rank matters less here than useful information and a paid table.

Interior: Compact dark-wood rooms with marble-topped tables, wall clocks, newspaper racks, coat hooks and a long counter. Seating is close enough that conversations frequently overlap.

Services: Strong coffee, tea, simple breakfasts, sandwiches, pastries and late afternoon food. Newspapers, public notices and message drops circulate constantly.

Information Ecology: Rumor, professional gossip, press talk, legal news and institutional complaints move rapidly through the room. Patrons may be informed, mistaken or deliberately misleading.

Atmosphere: Coffee, wet coats, ink, tobacco, newsprint, crowded voices and the constant opening of the street door.

Narrative Use: Good for informal contacts, journalists, overheard leads, quiet interviews, surveillance and meetings that should appear ordinary.

Information is abundant; reliability is not.
entries.description: Defines a busy Charter Ward coffee house frequented by clerks, journalists, investigators, lawyers and technical professionals.

entries.name: Alderwick — The Copper Lark Music Hall
entries.content:
Location: A large popular music hall on Velvet Row, near theatres, drinking houses and late-night carriage traffic.

Public Space: A broad auditorium with stage, gallery, private boxes and densely packed tables. Patrons drink, talk and react during performances rather than sitting in formal silence.

Entertainment: Singers, comic acts, dancers, acrobats, illusionists, novelty machinery demonstrations and touring performers. Programs change frequently.

Backstage: Dressing rooms, costume storage, fly systems, narrow stairs, loading access and service corridors form a second building hidden behind the public stage.

Clientele: Clerks, workers, travelers, performers, wealthy thrill-seekers and nightlife regulars mix more freely here than in formal theatres, though price still separates boxes from the gallery.

Atmosphere: Music, applause, smoke, perfume, beer, hot lamps, painted scenery, backstage dust and mechanical stage equipment.

Narrative Use: Excellent for covert meetings, tails lost in crowds, performer contacts, backstage infiltration, public distractions and information moving through nightlife workers.

The audience watches the stage while half the building watches the audience.
entries.description: Defines a large Velvet Row music hall combining popular entertainment, drinking, backstage labor and nightlife information.

entries.name: Alderwick — Saint Orison's Church
entries.content:
Location: An old parish church in Old Alderwick, within walking distance of Charter Ward and the older river streets.

Function: Active place of worship, marriage, burial services, charity and neighborhood gathering. It serves several social classes rather than belonging exclusively to the wealthy.

Architecture: Dark stone, worn steps, tall stained glass, timber pews, memorial tablets and an old bell tower. Later heating pipes, gas lamps and mechanical clockwork have been fitted into the medieval structure without erasing it.

Parish Life: Clergy and lay workers know local families, deaths, marriages, hardships, charitable requests and long-running neighborhood tensions. Parish records may preserve information unavailable elsewhere.

Atmosphere: Cold stone, wax, old wood, damp wool, incense at services, bell vibration and faint city smoke entering through opened doors.

Narrative Use: Useful for funerals, confidential conversations, parish records, sanctuary-like pauses, community witnesses and cases where old families intersect with ordinary residents.

The church remembers people long after the city stops noticing them.
entries.description: Defines an old active parish church in Old Alderwick serving worship, charity, records and neighborhood life.

entries.name: Alderwick — Saint Orison's Cemetery
entries.content:
Location: A large old cemetery beyond Saint Orison's Church at the edge of Old Alderwick, expanded repeatedly as the city grew.

Layout: Walled sections of winding paths, mature trees, family plots, common graves, stone monuments, mausoleums and newer industrial-era memorials. A keeper's lodge and small maintenance yard stand near the principal gate.

Social Geography: Wealth remains visible after death. Highwick families occupy elaborate plots and mausoleums; tradespeople have modest stones; poorer citizens may share dense common sections.

Access: Open during daylight and closed after dark except for staff, funerals or authorized entry. Old walls, secondary gates and maintenance routes make the perimeter imperfect rather than secure.

Atmosphere: Damp earth, stone, ivy, distant bells, soot on pale monuments and the muted industrial skyline beyond the trees.

Narrative Use: Suitable for funerals, clandestine meetings, grave records, hidden objects, surveillance, family history and discoveries tied to old identities or forgotten deaths.

Alderwick's class divisions continue into the landscape of the dead.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s large old garden cemetery beside Saint Orison’s parish, containing family monuments, common graves and service structures.

entries.name: Alderwick — The Rusted Anchor
entries.content:
Location: A crowded public house in Rookery near the road toward the older river crossings and worker housing.

Clientele: Dock laborers, factory hands, drivers, porters, tradespeople, off-duty constables and neighborhood regulars. Respectable outsiders can enter, but they are noticed.

Interior: Low ceilings, scarred timber tables, a long dark bar, coal stove, smoke-stained walls and a rear yard used for deliveries. A small upstairs room can be hired for private meetings.

Food & Drink: Ale, stout, spirits, meat pies, bread, cheese and simple hot meals. Service is fast rather than refined.

Social Function: Work gossip, hiring news, debts, arguments, rumors and local loyalties circulate here. Regulars often know more about neighborhood movements than official records do.

Atmosphere: Beer, coal smoke, wet wool, tobacco, fried food, loud conversation and the scrape of boots on old boards.

Narrative Use: Useful for labor contacts, informal witnesses, local rumors, covert meetings, following a suspect into working-class territory or learning what happened on a street after officials stopped watching.

The Anchor knows the neighborhood because the neighborhood drinks here.
entries.description: Defines a working-class Rookery public house serving laborers, drivers, dock workers and neighborhood regulars.

entries.name: Alderwick — The Meridian Club
entries.content:
Location: An exclusive private club in Bellmont, within easy reach of Highwick, banks and ministerial offices.

Membership: Aristocrats, senior officials, industrial leaders, financiers, barristers, military officers and established professionals. Entry normally requires membership or introduction by a member.

Interior: Quiet reading rooms, dining rooms, card tables, private parlors, a smoking room and a well-stocked library. Dark timber, leather chairs, restrained brass fittings and thick carpets suppress the noise of the street.

Services: Meals, drinks, newspapers, correspondence handling and private rooms for conversation. Staff are discreet and highly practiced at remembering members without appearing to observe them.

Social Function: The club converts reputation into access. Alliances, introductions, favors and decisions often begin here before becoming formal elsewhere.

Atmosphere: Tobacco, leather, old paper, polished wood, low voices, firelight and mechanical clocks.

Narrative Use: Best for elite contacts, political gossip, industrial negotiation, discreet observation and cases where access depends on invitation rather than legal authority.

Membership opens doors, but every door belongs to someone.
entries.description: Defines an exclusive Bellmont gentlemen’s club used by aristocrats, industrial leaders, senior officials and wealthy professionals.

entries.name: Alderwick — Veyne Central Market
entries.content:
Location: A vast covered market on the Rookery side of the Veyne, connected by busy streets to Grey Quays, worker districts and the bridge routes.

Function: Principal market for food, household goods, flowers, meat, fish and everyday trade. Wholesale activity begins before dawn; retail crowds dominate later in the morning.

Layout: Iron-and-glass roof, long aisles of permanent stalls, loading courts, cold stores, butcher sections, produce halls and service passages. Handcarts, small hoists and delivery machinery operate constantly.

Clientele: Traders, servants, cooks, workers, households, porters, street sellers and buyers from nearly every social layer. Wealth changes what is purchased, not who may enter.

Information Ecology: Stallholders and porters see deliveries, unusual customers, sudden shortages, disputes and changes in routine. Market knowledge is practical, immediate and highly local.

Atmosphere: Voices, wheels, livestock, wet stone, vegetables, flowers, blood, fish, bread, coal smoke and morning condensation on the glass roof.

Narrative Use: Useful for witnesses, pursuit through crowds, disguised meetings, tracking goods, tracing deliveries, discovering shortages or finding someone who notices patterns because business depends on them.

If something enters Alderwick through ordinary trade, someone at the market has probably seen it.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s major covered market as a crowded cross-class hub of food, trade, deliveries and street information.

entries.name: Alderwick — Central Telegraph & General Post Office
entries.content:
Location: A large civic communications building in Charter Ward near government offices, commercial streets and routes toward Bracken Cross.

Function: Alderwick's principal hub for postal sorting, registered mail, telegram transmission, official dispatches and routing between local offices, rail services and external lines.

Public Hall: Counters handle letters, parcels, telegram forms, payments, registration and collection. Clerks work behind high desks under large route clocks and notice boards.

Operational Areas: Sorting rooms, telegraph galleries, message dispatch desks, secure registered-mail storage, staff corridors and loading access connect to rail and courier services. Public access does not extend into these areas.

Technology: Telegraph instruments, message tubes, mechanical timestamps, sorting racks, route clocks and secure document cabinets operate continuously. Systems record transmission and handling but do not make messages private or impossible to intercept.

Information & Privacy: Clerks, operators, couriers and sorting staff may know that a message or parcel passed through the system, though not every worker knows its contents. Records can establish timing, origin, destination and handling chain when access is lawfully or covertly obtained.

Atmosphere: Paper, ink, sealing wax, damp coats, brass instruments, ticking clocks, telegraph clicks, pneumatic knocks and hurried footsteps.

Narrative Use: Ideal for tracing telegrams, missing correspondence, forged dispatches, intercepted mail, timing alibis, surveillance of couriers and investigations where communication infrastructure becomes evidence.

Alderwick's messages move quickly, but they leave traces.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s main telegraph and postal hub in Charter Ward, handling messages, mail, official dispatches and routing records.

entries.name: Alderwick — Bell & Thistle Apothecary
entries.content:
Location: A respected pharmacy and apothecary in Charter Ward, serving professionals, households, servants, Bureau staff and nearby residents.

Function: Dispenses physician prescriptions, compounds medicines, sells common remedies and supplies limited chemical and medical goods. It is a normal commercial medical business, not an illicit drug den.

Interior: Dark wooden cabinets, labeled drawers, glass bottles, brass scales, ceramic jars, measuring equipment and a rear compounding room behind the public counter.

Records: Prescription ledgers, account books, order notes and supplier invoices may establish that a medicine or chemical was dispensed, when, in what quantity and under whose account. Records may be incomplete, mistaken, forged or associated with a purchaser acting for someone else.

Professional Knowledge: The apothecary can identify common preparations, unusual dosages, dangerous combinations, suspicious substitutions and whether a claimed medicine matches ordinary practice.

Access: Opiate preparations, sedatives, stimulants and potent compounds may be legitimately supplied when medically or commercially appropriate. Regular purchase may indicate treatment, dependence, household use or resale; it does not prove criminal intent.

Atmosphere: Dried herbs, alcohol, medicinal oils, soap, paper labels, polished wood and the sharp chemical smell of the compounding room.

Narrative Use: Useful for tracing medicines, identifying compounds, reconstructing purchase history, finding supplier links, testing alibis and distinguishing legitimate treatment from suspicious access.

The pharmacy can show how a substance moved; it cannot automatically show why.
entries.description: Defines a respected Charter Ward pharmacy and apothecary serving ordinary medical needs while generating useful prescription, purchase and chemical evidence.

entries.name: Alderwick — Veyne Royal Infirmary
entries.content:
Location: A large charitable and teaching hospital between Charter Ward and the older commercial streets, accessible from both central districts and worker neighborhoods.

Function: Treats industrial injuries, illness, surgery, poisoning, childbirth complications and serious emergencies. Wealthy patients may use private rooms; most citizens are treated in shared wards.

Layout: Reception hall, general wards, surgical rooms, private rooms, dispensary, kitchens, laundry, mortuary, records office and service corridors. Older stone wings have been repeatedly adapted with pipes, lifts, heating and medical machinery.

Medicine: Surgery, anesthesia, antiseptic practice, basic laboratory chemistry and practical toxicology are established but imperfect. Diagnosis depends on symptoms, examination, history and limited tests rather than modern certainty.

Records: Admission books, physician notes, treatment records and mortuary documentation can establish timing, reported symptoms and care received. Records may contain errors, incomplete histories or conclusions later proved wrong.

Staff: Physicians, surgeons, nurses, orderlies, clerks, porters and students each see different parts of a patient's story. Social rank affects privacy and comfort more than the physical reality of injury or disease.

Atmosphere: Carbolic disinfectant, soap, steam heat, linen, medicine, metal instruments, footsteps, bells and the constant mixture of recovery, exhaustion and emergency.

Narrative Use: Useful for injured witnesses, poisoning cases, disputed causes of death, medical secrets, false identities, missing patients, staff testimony and determining whether an apparent crime may have a medical explanation.

The hospital records suffering; it does not guarantee certainty about its cause.
entries.description: Defines Alderwick’s major public teaching hospital, treating accident, illness, surgery and poisoning across social classes while maintaining imperfect medical records.
